audioscript.text: Section 4.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You will hear part of a lecture to business students about the use of one particular type of research known as ethnography.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully, and answer questions 31 to 40.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: So what I'm going to talk about to you today is something called ethnography.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This is a type of research aimed at exploring the way human cultures work.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It was first developed for use in anthropology, and it's also been used in sociology and communication studies.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: So, what's it got to do with business?
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: You may ask.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Well, businesses are finding that ethnography can offer them deeper insight into the possible needs of customers, either present or future, as well as providing valuable information about their attitudes towards existing products.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q31: The passage says ethnography gives *'valuable information about their attitudes towards existing products'* — the question asks about customer needs and **attitudes**. So the answer is **attitudes**.

audioscript.text: And ethnography can also help companies to design new products or services that customers really want.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Let's look at some examples of how ethnographic research works in business.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: One team of researchers did a project for a company manufacturing kitchen equipment.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: They watched how cooks used measuring cups to measure out things like sugar and flour.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: They saw that the cooks had to check and recheck the contents.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Because although the measuring cups had numbers inside them, the cooks couldn't see these easily.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q32: The passage says *'the measuring cups had numbers inside them, the cooks couldn't see these easily'* — the cooks could not see the **numbers**. So the answer is **numbers**.

audioscript.text: So, a new design of cup was developed to overcome this problem.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And it was a top seller.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Another team of ethnographic researchers looked at how cell phones were used in Uganda in Africa.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: They found that people who didn't have their own phones could pay to use the phones of local entrepreneurs, because these customers paid in advance for their calls.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: They were eager to know how much time they'd spent on the call so far.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q33: The passage says customers *'were eager to know how much time they'd spent on the call so far'* — they wanted to check the **time** used. So the answer is **time**.

audioscript.text: So the phone company designed phones for use globally with this added feature.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Ethnographic research has also been carried out in computer companies.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: In one company, IT systems administrators were observed for several weeks.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It was found that a large amount of their work involved communicating with colleagues in order to solve problems, but that they didn't have a standard way of exchanging information from spreadsheets and so on.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: So, the team came up with an idea for software that would help them to do this.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q34: The passage says *'the team came up with an idea for software that would help them to do this'* — they needed to develop **software** to improve communication. So the answer is **software**.

audioscript.text: In another piece of research, a team observed and talked to nurses working in hospitals.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This led to the recognition that the nurses needed to access the computer records of their patients, no matter where they were.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q35: The passage says nurses needed *'to access the computer records of their patients'* — they needed information about **patients**. So the answer is **patients**.

audioscript.text: This led to the development of a portable computer tablet that allowed the nurses to check records in locations throughout the hospital.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Occasionally, research can be done even in environments where the researchers can't be present.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: For example, in one project done for an airline.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Respondents used their smartphones to record information during airline trips, in a study aiming at tracking the emotions of passengers during a flight.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q36: The passage says the study aimed at *'tracking the emotions of passengers during a flight'* — respondents recorded their **emotions** while travelling. So the answer is **emotions**.

audioscript.text: So, what makes studies like these different from ordinary research?
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Let's look at some of the general principles behind ethnographic research in business.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: First of all, the researcher has to be completely open-minded.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: He or she hasn't thought up a hypothesis to be tested, as is the case in other types of research.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Instead, they wait for the participants in the research to inform them.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: As far as choosing the participants themselves is concerned, that's not really all that different from ordinary research.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The criteria according to which the participants are chosen may be something as simple as the age bracket they fall into, or the researchers may select them according to their income.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q37: The passage says participants may be chosen by *'the age bracket they fall into, or the researchers may select them according to their income'* — the missing criterion is **income**. So the answer is **income**.

audioscript.text: Or they might try to find a set of people who all use a particular product for example, but it's absolutely crucial to recruit the right people as participants.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: As well as the criteria I've mentioned, they have to be comfortable talking about themselves, and being watched as they go about their activities.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q38: The passage says participants *'have to be comfortable talking about themselves, and being watched'* — they must feel **comfortable** about taking part. So the answer is **comfortable**.

audioscript.text: Actually, most researchers say that people open up pretty easily.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Maybe because they're often in their own home or workplace.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: So, what makes this type of research special is that it's not just a matter of sending a questionnaire to the participants.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Instead, the research is usually based on first-hand observation of what they are doing at the time.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q39: The passage says research is *'based on first-hand observation of what they are doing'* — there is usually direct **observation** of the participants. So the answer is **observation**.

audioscript.text: But that doesn't mean that the researcher never talks to the participants.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: However, unlike in traditional research, in this case, it's the participant rather than the researchers who decides what direction the interview will follow.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This means that there's less likelihood of the researcher imposing his or her own ideas on the participant.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: But after they've said goodbye to their participants and got back to their office, the researcher's work isn't finished.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Most researchers estimate that 70 to 80% of their time is spent not on the collecting of data, but on its analysis, looking at photos, listening to recordings and transcribing them, and so on.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q40: The passage says *'70 to 80% of their time is spent not on the collecting of data, but on its analysis'* — a lot of time is needed for the **analysis** of the data. So the answer is **analysis**.

audioscript.text: The researchers may end up with hundreds of pages of notes, and to determine what's significant, they don't focus on the sensational things or the unusual things.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Instead, they try to identify a pattern of some sort in all this data, and to discern the meaning behind it.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This can result in some compelling insights.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: That can in turn feed back to the whole design process.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: That is the end of Section 4.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Section 4.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You will hear part of a lecture about a way of reducing the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully, and answer questions 31 to 40.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: As we saw in the last lecture, a major cause of climate change is the rapid rise in the level of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere over the last century.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: If we could reduce the amount of CO₂, perhaps the rate of climate change could also be slowed down.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: One potential method involves enhancing the role of the soil that plants grow in.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: With regard to absorbing CO₂.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Rattan Lal, a soil scientist from Ohio State University in the USA, claims that the world's agricultural soils could potentially absorb 13% of the carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, the equivalent of the amount released in the last 30 years.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And research is going on into how this might be achieved.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Lal first came to the idea that soil might be valuable in this way, not through an interest in climate change, but rather out of concern for the land itself, and the people dependent on it.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Carbon rich soil is dark, crumbly and fertile, and retains some water.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: But erosion can occur if soil is dry, which is a likely effect.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q31: The passage says *'erosion can occur if soil is dry'* — **'dry'** is the condition that makes erosion more likely. So the answer is **dry**.

audioscript.text: If it contains inadequate amounts of carbon, erosion is of course bad for people trying to grow crops or breed animals on that terrain.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: In the 1970s and '80s, Lal was studying soils in Africa, so devoid of organic matter that the ground had become extremely hard.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q32: The passage says Lal found soil in Africa *'so devoid of organic matter that the ground had become extremely hard'* — **'extremely hard'** means very **hard**. So the answer is **hard**.

audioscript.text: Like cement, there he met a pioneer in the study of global warming, who suggested that carbon from the soil had moved into the atmosphere.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This is now looking increasingly likely.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Let me explain.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: For millions of years, carbon dioxide levels in the atmosphere have been regulated in part by a natural partnership between plants and microbes, tiny organisms in the soil.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Plants absorb CO₂ from the air, and transform it into sugars and other carbon-based substances.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q33: The passage says plants *'transform it into sugars and other carbon-based substances'* — **'sugars'** is the example of a carbon-based substance. So the answer is **sugars**.

audioscript.text: While a proportion of these carbon products remain in the plant, some transfer from the roots to fungi and soil microbes, which store the carbon in the soil.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q34: The passage says *'some transfer from the roots to fungi and soil microbes'* — the CO₂ moves from the **roots** of plants. So the answer is **roots**.

audioscript.text: The invention of agriculture some 10,000 years ago disrupted these ancient soil-building processes and led to the loss of carbon from the soil.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: When humans started draining the natural topsoil and plowing it up for planting, they exposed the buried carbon to oxygen.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This created carbon dioxide and released it into the air, and in some places, grazing by domesticated animals has removed all vegetation, releasing carbon into the air.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Tons of carbon have been stripped from the world's soils where it's needed, and pumped into the atmosphere.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: So, what can be done?
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Researchers are now coming up with evidence that even modest changes to farming can significantly help to reduce the amount of carbon in the atmosphere.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Some growers have already started using an approach known as regenerative agriculture.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This aims to boost the fertility of soil and keep it moist through established practices.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q35: The passage says regenerative agriculture aims to *'keep it moist'* — **'moist'** means slightly wet, which is the same as fertile and **moist**. So the answer is **moist**.

audioscript.text: These include keeping fields planted all year round, and increasing the variety of plants being grown.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q36: The passage says practices include *'increasing the variety of plants being grown'* — **'variety'** means different types. So the answer is **variety**.

audioscript.text: Strategies like these can significantly increase the amount of carbon stored in the soil, so agricultural researchers are now building a case for their use in combating climate change.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: One American investigation into the potential for storing CO₂ on agricultural lands is taking place in California.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Soil scientist Whendee Silver of the University of California, Berkeley is conducting a first-of-its-kind study on a large cattle farm in the state.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q37: The passage says the study is *'on a large cattle farm'* — **'cattle'** means cows, so it is a big **cattle** farm. So the answer is **cattle**.

audioscript.text: She and her students are testing the effects on carbon storage of the compost that is created from waste.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q38: The passage says compost is made from *'waste produced in gardens'* — **'gardens'** is the source of waste like leaves. So the answer is **gardens**.

audioscript.text: Both agricultural, including manure and cornstalks, and waste produced in gardens, such as leaves, branches, and lawn trimmings.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q38: The passage says compost is made from *'waste produced in gardens'* — **'gardens'** is the source of waste like leaves. So the answer is **gardens**.

audioscript.text: In Australia, soil ecologist Christine Jones is testing another promising soil enrichment strategy.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Jones and 12 farmers are working to build up soil carbon by cultivating grasses that stay green all year round.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q39: The passage says they are *'cultivating grasses that stay green all year round'* — **'grasses'** are the plants used to increase soil carbon. So the answer is **grasses**.

audioscript.text: Like composting, the approach has already been proved experimentally.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Jones now hopes to show that it can be applied on working farms, and that the resulting carbon capture can be accurately measured.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It's hoped in the future that projects such as these will demonstrate the role that farmers and other land managers can play in reducing the harmful effects of greenhouse gases.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: For example, in countries like the United States, where most farming operations use large applications of fertilizer, changing such long standing habits will require a change of system.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Rattan Lal argues that farmers should receive payment, not just for the corn or beef they produce, but also for the carbon they can store in their soil.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q40: The passage says *'farmers should receive payment'* for carbon storage — **'payment'** means money given for a service. So the answer is **payment**.

audioscript.text: Another study being carried out.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: That is the end of Section 4.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER
